title: Chapter 8 — Queries, Modeling, and Transformation: Quality Question Bank

questions.question: What are DDL, DML, DCL, and TCL, and what's one example command from each?
options: DDL defines database objects (CREATE, DROP); DML manipulates data (SELECT, INSERT); DCL controls access (GRANT, REVOKE); TCL controls transactions (COMMIT, ROLLBACK)
DDL manipulates data; DML defines objects; DCL controls transactions; TCL controls access
All four acronyms refer to the same set of SQL commands under different vendor names
DCL and TCL are deprecated terms no longer used in modern SQL databases
questions.explanation: The book walks through each in turn: DDL (CREATE/DROP/UPDATE for objects), DML (SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE for data), DCL (GRANT/DENY/REVOKE for access), and TCL (COMMIT/ROLLBACK for transactions).

questions.question: In the "life of a query," what does the query optimizer do?
options: After the SQL is compiled into bytecode, the optimizer analyzes it to determine the most efficient execution plan, reordering and refactoring steps to use resources efficiently
It converts SQL directly into a data warehouse's storage engine, skipping compilation entirely
It runs only after query execution completes, purely to log statistics
It exists solely to enforce access control permissions (DCL)
questions.explanation: The book's four-step summary places the optimizer after compilation: it "analyzes the bytecode to determine how to execute the query, reordering and refactoring steps to use available resources as efficiently as possible."

questions.question: A join key value repeats 5 times in table A and 10 times in table B, producing far more output rows than expected for that value alone. What's this called, and why is it dangerous?
options: Row explosion — the many-to-many match creates a cross-join effect (5×10=50 rows for that key), which can consume massive resources or crash a query, especially before a filtering predicate is applied
This is called "normalization drift" and only affects storage costs, not query resources
It's called a "broadcast join" and is always beneficial for performance
It only happens in row-oriented databases, never in columnar ones
questions.explanation: The book defines this exactly: "This creates 5 × 10 = 50 rows in the output... Row explosion often generates enough rows to consume a massive quantity of database resources or even cause a query to fail."

questions.question: How do BigQuery's and PostgreSQL's commit/consistency models differ for analytics queries, per the book?
options: PostgreSQL uses row locking with ACID transactions, which can block reads/writes and isn't optimized for huge scans; BigQuery uses point-in-time full-table snapshots (no locking) but allows only one write operation at a time
PostgreSQL uses point-in-time snapshots while BigQuery uses row locking
Both databases use an identical commit model
PostgreSQL allows unlimited concurrent writes while BigQuery allows none, ever, under any condition
questions.explanation: The book contrasts PostgreSQL's row-locking ACID transactions ("not optimized for large scans") with BigQuery's snapshot reads plus "no write concurrency whatsoever" for a single table at a time.

questions.question: Why does the book describe MongoDB's high-write-performance mode as risky for some applications?
options: Under heavy load, it can silently and unceremoniously discard writes — fine for tolerant use cases like some IoT measurements, but bad for applications needing exact data capture
MongoDB always requires manual conflict resolution for every single write operation
MongoDB cannot support any write concurrency at all in any configuration
MongoDB silently duplicates every write rather than discarding any of them
questions.explanation: The book states: "the database will unceremoniously and silently discard writes if it gets overwhelmed with traffic... not a great fit for applications that need to capture exact data and statistics."

questions.question: What is "vacuuming" in a database, and why does it matter beyond freeing disk space?
options: Vacuuming removes dead/obsolete records left behind by updates and deletes — it also keeps query plans accurate (stale records can mislead the optimizer) and keeps indexes performant
Vacuuming only ever affects disk space and has no other meaningful side effects
Vacuuming is a required step before any SELECT query can be executed
Vacuuming permanently disables any future updates to the affected table
questions.explanation: The book lists three reasons: freeing space for faster queries, "query plans are more accurate" since outdated records mislead the optimizer, and cleaning up indexes for better performance.

questions.question: What's the "fast-follower" CDC pattern for streaming queries, and what's its key limitation compared to the Kappa architecture?
options: Fast-follower sets up an analytics database as a lagging CDC-fed replica, queried with ordinary SELECTs; its limitation is it doesn't let you trigger events directly off stream changes, unlike Kappa, which treats the stream itself as the queryable store
Fast-follower requires no production database at all to function
Kappa architecture cannot support any historical queries, only fast-follower can
Fast-follower and Kappa are simply two names for the identical architecture
questions.explanation: The book states fast-follower "doesn't fundamentally rethink batch query patterns... missing the opportunity to dynamically trigger events off changes in the stream," unlike Kappa's stream-as-database approach.

questions.question: What's the difference between a fixed-time (tumbling) window and a sliding window in stream processing?
options: A tumbling window processes all data since the previous window closed with no overlap; a sliding window has fixed-length windows that can overlap (e.g. a new 60-second window every 30 seconds)
Tumbling windows always overlap, while sliding windows never do
Both window types are identical, just named differently by different streaming vendors
Tumbling windows only apply to batch data, never to true streaming data
questions.explanation: The book describes tumbling windows as running "on a fixed schedule and process[ing] all data since the previous window is closed," versus sliding windows where "separate windows might overlap," giving the 60-second/30-second example.

questions.question: What is a "watermark" in stream processing, and what does it determine?
options: A threshold a window uses to decide whether incoming data falls within its time interval or should be treated as late-arriving
A security label applied automatically to sensitive streaming data
A checkpoint used only for exactly-once delivery guarantees
A compression marker inserted periodically into Kafka topics
questions.explanation: The book defines it directly: "A watermark is a threshold used by a window to determine whether data in a window is within the established time interval or whether it's considered late."

questions.question: What are the three levels of the data modeling continuum, and what does each add?
options: Conceptual (business logic/entities via an ER diagram) → logical (adds types, primary/foreign keys) → physical (adds concrete databases, schemas, tables, and configuration)
Physical → logical → conceptual, moving from concrete implementation toward abstract business rules
Logical → physical → conceptual, with conceptual as the final implementation stage
There are only two levels in the book's continuum: conceptual and physical
questions.explanation: The book defines this continuum explicitly in that order: conceptual (business logic, ER diagrams), logical (adds types and keys), then physical (adds concrete database implementation details).

questions.question: The book advises modeling data "at the lowest level of grain possible," even when the immediate request is for a coarse daily summary. Why?
options: You can always aggregate up from fine-grained data, but detail generally can't be recovered once it's been aggregated away — so fine grain preserves flexibility for future requests
Fine-grained data is always cheaper to store than any aggregated summary table
Coarse-grained data cannot be queried using SQL at all
The book actually recommends the opposite: always model at the coarsest grain first
questions.explanation: The book states: "you should strive to model your data at the lowest level of grain possible. From here, it's easy to aggregate this highly granular dataset. The reverse isn't true."

questions.question: In the book's normalization walkthrough, "Sku determines ProductName" even though ProductName isn't part of the composite primary key. What problem is this, and what normal form fixes it?
options: A transitive dependency (a nonkey field depends on another nonkey field) — resolved by splitting the table further to reach third normal form (3NF)
A partial dependency, which is fixed simply by reaching first normal form (1NF)
This isn't a normalization issue at all, just a naming-convention choice
It's fixed by denormalizing the table further, moving away from 3NF entirely
questions.explanation: The book identifies exactly this: "Sku depends on the composite key, and ProductName depends on Sku. This is a transitive dependency," resolved by splitting into further tables to reach 3NF.

questions.question: How does Inmon's data warehouse approach fundamentally differ from Kimball's, in structure and direction?
options: Inmon integrates data from across the business into a highly normalized (3NF) central warehouse first, then serves department-specific star schemas via downstream data marts; Kimball is bottom-up, serving analytics directly in the warehouse via denormalized star schemas
Kimball integrates all business data into a normalized warehouse first, while Inmon builds star schemas directly with no central warehouse
Both approaches are functionally identical, differing only in publication decade
Inmon's model has no concept of a data mart at all — only Kimball uses data marts
questions.explanation: The book contrasts them directly: Inmon's warehouse is highly normalized with department analytics served via data marts, while "the Kimball model is bottom-up... effectively mak[ing] the data mart the data warehouse itself."

questions.question: In Kimball's star schema, what's the difference between a fact table and a dimension table?
options: Fact tables hold immutable, quantitative, event-level data (narrow, many rows, append-only, lowest grain); dimension tables hold descriptive, denormalized reference attributes (wide, fewer rows) that give context to facts
Fact tables are always denormalized, while dimension tables are always strictly normalized
Both table types are functionally identical within a star schema
Dimension tables hold quantitative data, while fact tables hold descriptive attributes
questions.explanation: The book states fact tables are "factual, quantitative, and event-related... narrow and long," while dimension tables "provide the reference data, attributes, and relational context... typically wide and short."

questions.question: What's a Type 2 slowly changing dimension (SCD), and how does it differ from Type 1?
options: Type 2 inserts a new row with updated attributes (closing the old row's effective end date) to preserve full history; Type 1 simply overwrites the existing record, losing history
Type 1 preserves full history via new rows, while Type 2 overwrites records in place
Type 1 always uses more storage than Type 2, since it retains every historical version
Type 2 is usable only for date dimensions, never for customer dimensions
questions.explanation: The book defines Type 1 as "overwrite existing dimension records... no access to the deleted historical records" and Type 2 as keeping "a full history of dimension records" via new inserted rows.

questions.question: In a Data Vault model, what are hubs, links, and satellites respectively responsible for?
options: Hubs store unique business keys; links track many-to-many relationships between hubs; satellites hold descriptive attributes/context tied to a hub or link
Hubs store descriptive attributes; links store business keys; satellites track relationships between hubs
Satellites store business keys; hubs hold descriptive context; links are purely optional metadata
All three table types serve the exact same purpose in a Data Vault
questions.explanation: The book states directly: "a hub stores business keys, a link maintains relationships among business keys, and a satellite represents a business key's attributes and context."

questions.question: Why do wide, sparse denormalized tables work well in columnar databases but poorly in traditional relational databases?
options: Columnar databases only read the columns actually selected and store nulls essentially for free, while relational databases allocate fixed space per field and must read each row's full contents
Wide tables are equally efficient in both database types, with no real difference
Wide tables can only exist in relational databases, never in columnar ones
Nulls are more expensive to store in columnar databases than in relational databases
questions.explanation: The book explains: "nulls take up virtually no space in a columnar database" while a wide schema in a relational database "dramatically slows reading because each row must allocate all the space specified by the wide schema."

questions.question: What's the difference between a broadcast join and a shuffle hash join in distributed query processing?
options: A broadcast join sends a small table to every node to join against a large distributed table (cheap); a shuffle hash join repartitions both tables by join key across the cluster when neither is small enough to broadcast (more resource-intensive)
Broadcast joins are always more expensive to run than shuffle hash joins
Shuffle hash joins only work on a single node and cannot be distributed
Broadcast joins require both tables to be equally large before they can run
questions.explanation: The book explains broadcast joins as sending a small table to all nodes ("far less compute intensive"), while shuffle hash joins repartition both tables by key when "neither table is small enough to fit on a single node."

questions.question: What's the difference between a "hard delete" and a "soft delete," and when might "insert deletion" be used instead?
options: A hard delete permanently removes a record; a soft delete marks it as deleted but keeps it in place; insert deletion adds a new record flagged as deleted without touching the previous version, at the cost of a more complex current-state query
Hard deletes are always reversible, while soft deletes are permanent and irreversible
Insert deletion physically removes all prior versions of a record immediately
Soft deletes and hard deletes are two names for exactly the same operation
questions.explanation: The book defines a hard delete as permanently removing a record and a soft delete as marking it deleted while filtering it from results, then describes insert deletion as inserting "a new record with a deleted flag without modifying the previous version."

questions.question: Why does the book warn against running near-real-time merge/upsert operations against a columnar cloud data warehouse at the same frequency that worked on an old row-based system?
options: Columnar systems rely on copy-on-write, so frequent small merges force expensive file rewrites — teams that tried this saw systems "fall weeks behind," and a less frequent cadence (e.g. hourly) usually works far better
Columnar warehouses cannot perform merges under any circumstances whatsoever
Merge frequency has no meaningful performance implications in any database type
This concern only applies to row-based databases, never to columnar ones
questions.explanation: The book states plainly: "No matter how good your CDC system is, this approach will bring most columnar data warehouses to their knees. We've seen systems fall weeks behind on updates."

questions.question: What's the difference between a (nonmaterialized) view and a materialized view?
options: A view is a stored query definition recomputed every time it's selected from; a materialized view precomputes and stores the result in advance, refreshed as source data changes, trading storage/freshness for faster reads
Materialized views never need to be refreshed once they're initially created
Views can reference only a single table, while materialized views can reference many tables
A materialized view and a regular view are functionally identical concepts
questions.explanation: The book explains: a view "is just a query that references other tables" recomputed on selection, while "a materialized view does some or all of the view computation in advance," saving results as source tables change.

questions.question: What's the practical difference between micro-batching and "true streaming" processing, and how does the book suggest choosing between them?
options: Micro-batching applies a batch-oriented framework at short, frequent intervals, while true streaming processes one event at a time with more overhead — the choice should be driven by actual latency requirements and team expertise, not by dismissing micro-batch as inherently inferior
True streaming is always slower than micro-batching, regardless of the use case
Micro-batching is physically incapable of running more often than once per day
The book insists true streaming is always the objectively correct engineering choice
questions.explanation: The book states: "The term micro-batch has often been used to dismiss competing technologies, but it may work just fine for your use case," and recommends matching the choice to acceptable latency and existing team expertise.

questions.question: How does the book define a query, and how does it relate to CRUD?
options: A query allows you to retrieve and act on data; retrieving is the R (read) in CRUD, and queries can also create, mutate, or destroy existing records (the CUD)
A query can only ever read data, never modify it
Queries have no relationship to CRUD operations
A query is the same thing as a database index
questions.explanation: The book says a query retrieves data (R in CRUD) and can also create, mutate, or destroy records (CUD), e.g. SELECT * FROM foo WHERE id=1.

questions.question: What is the purpose of data definition language (DDL), and what example does the book give?
options: DDL performs operations on database objects such as the database, schemas, tables, or users, defining the state of objects — e.g. CREATE DATABASE bar or DROP TABLE bar_table
DDL controls user access permissions
DDL manages transactions and rollbacks
DDL only runs SELECT queries
questions.explanation: The book says DDL defines the state of objects in your database with commands like CREATE, DROP, and UPDATE, giving CREATE DATABASE bar as an example.

questions.question: What DML commands does the book list for a data engineer?
options: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, COPY, and MERGE
CREATE, DROP, ALTER, and RENAME
GRANT, DENY, and REVOKE
COMMIT and ROLLBACK
questions.explanation: The book lists SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, COPY, and MERGE as common DML commands.

questions.question: What is data control language (DCL), and what example does the book give?
options: DCL controls access to database objects or data using commands such as GRANT, DENY, and REVOKE — e.g. GRANT SELECT ON data_science_db TO Sarah, then later REVOKE SELECT when she leaves
DCL defines table structures
DCL inserts and updates rows
DCL commits and rolls back transactions
questions.explanation: The book uses the Sarah example of granting then revoking read-only access with GRANT/REVOKE.

questions.question: What is transaction control language (TCL), and what do its commands do?
options: TCL supports commands controlling transaction details, defining commit checkpoints and conditions when actions roll back — common commands are COMMIT and ROLLBACK
TCL defines database schemas
TCL grants database access
TCL runs analytical SELECT queries
questions.explanation: The book says TCL defines commit checkpoints and rollback conditions with COMMIT and ROLLBACK.

questions.question: What is the first step in the "life of a query"?
options: The database engine compiles the SQL, parsing the code to check for proper semantics, ensuring referenced objects exist, and confirming the current user has appropriate access
The optimizer reorders the query steps
Results are produced immediately
The storage engine scans the entire table
questions.explanation: The book's first step is compilation/parsing with semantics, object-existence, and access checks.

questions.question: What happens in the second step of the "life of a query"?
options: The SQL code is converted into bytecode expressing the steps to be executed on the database engine in an efficient, machine-readable format
The query results are cached
The query optimizer analyzes the bytecode
Access permissions are revoked
questions.explanation: The book says the SQL is converted into bytecode in step two.

questions.question: What is the query optimizer's job, and what factors does it assess?
options: To optimize query performance and minimize costs by breaking the query into appropriate steps in an efficient order, assessing joins, indexes, data scan size, and other factors
To enforce database security permissions
To physically write data to disk
To render query results in a dashboard
questions.explanation: The book says the optimizer attempts to execute the query in the least expensive manner, assessing joins, indexes, and scan size.

questions.question: What does the book recommend about understanding your database's query optimizer?
options: You won't directly work with the optimizer, but understanding its functionality helps you write more performant queries, using tools like an explain plan or query analysis
You must rewrite the optimizer yourself
The optimizer is irrelevant to query performance
Optimizers are identical across all databases
questions.explanation: The book says engineers won't work with the optimizer directly but should understand it and use explain plans.

questions.question: What performance technique does the book recommend when analytics queries join the same data repeatedly?
options: Prejoin the data in advance and have queries read the prejoined version, possibly widening tables and using arrays or structs, or maintaining normalized schemas with prejoined tables for common use cases
Never prejoin data
Always query the raw source directly
Prejoining is always slower
questions.explanation: The book recommends prejoining repeatedly joined data to avoid repeating computationally intensive work.

questions.question: How does the book say PostgreSQL can index computed results, and why is this useful?
options: PostgreSQL allows creating an index on a string field converted to lowercase; when a query uses lower() in a predicate, the optimizer can apply the index
PostgreSQL cannot index computed results
Indexes can only be created on primary keys
Computed indexes always slow queries down
questions.explanation: The book gives the lowercase-string index as an example of indexing computed results.

questions.question: Why does the book recommend common table expressions (CTEs) over nested subqueries or temporary tables?
options: CTEs allow composing complex queries in a readable fashion, helping you understand query flow, and in many cases deliver better performance than creating intermediate tables
CTEs are always slower than temporary tables
CTEs cannot be composed into complex queries
Readability is unimportant for complex queries
questions.explanation: The book recommends CTEs for readability and often better performance than intermediate tables.

questions.question: What does an explain plan show, and how is it accessed?
options: It shows how the optimizer determined its optimum lowest-cost query, the database objects used, and resource/performance statistics per stage; some databases provide it visually and others via SQL with the EXPLAIN command
It shows only the query's syntax errors
It is a security audit log
It cannot be accessed by users
questions.explanation: The book describes the explain plan's contents and the EXPLAIN command/visual access.

questions.question: What metrics does the book suggest monitoring for query performance?
options: Usage of key resources (disk, memory, network), data loading vs processing time, query execution time/records/scan size/data shuffled, competing queries causing contention, and concurrent connections used vs available
Only the number of tables
Only the database version number
Query performance cannot be monitored
questions.explanation: The book lists these monitoring areas, including oversubscribed concurrent connections.

questions.question: Why is running SELECT * with no predicates inefficient, especially on pay-as-you-go databases?
options: It scans the entire table retrieving every row and column, which is expensive when the database charges for bytes scanned or compute resources utilized
SELECT * is always the fastest query
Scanning is always free
It returns only the columns you need
questions.explanation: The book says SELECT * scans everything and is very inefficient and expensive on pay-as-you-go databases.

questions.question: What pruning strategies does the book recommend for columnar versus row-oriented databases?
options: Columnar: select only needed columns and use tools like cluster keys (Snowflake/BigQuery) and partitioning; row-oriented: create table indexes for performance-sensitive queries without overloading the table
Columnar databases use indexes; row-oriented use cluster keys
Pruning is never recommended
Both database types use identical pruning
questions.explanation: The book contrasts columnar column-selection/cluster-key/partitioning pruning with row-oriented index strategies.

questions.question: What is a database commit, and what is the purpose of a transaction?
options: A commit is a change such as creating, updating, or deleting a record or object; transactions commit several operations simultaneously to maintain a consistent state and handle isolation during concurrent reads/writes/deletes
A commit only deletes data
Transactions cannot maintain consistency
Isolation is handled without transactions
questions.explanation: The book defines commits/transactions and their role in consistency and isolation.

questions.question: What is a dirty read, and why should engineers know if their database allows them?
options: A dirty read happens when a row is read after an uncommitted transaction has altered it — engineers should know if this is expected behavior and how to handle it, since queries may return unexpected results without ACID compliance
A dirty read is a performance optimization
Dirty reads never happen in databases
Dirty reads guarantee consistent results
questions.explanation: The book warns about dirty reads from uncommitted transactions and non-ACID behavior.

questions.question: What does the book say about BigQuery's point-in-time full-table commit model?
options: A read query reads from the latest committed snapshot and will not see subsequent changes even if it runs for hours; BigQuery does not lock the table, and write operations create new commits/snapshots
BigQuery locks the table during reads
Reads see all future changes
BigQuery has no snapshots
questions.explanation: The book describes BigQuery's snapshot-read model with no locking and new snapshots on writes.

questions.question: How does BigQuery handle concurrent write operations?
options: It allows only one write operation at a time — providing no write concurrency in that sense — and queues write queries in order of arrival if multiple clients write simultaneously
It allows unlimited concurrent writes
It rejects all writes
It merges all concurrent writes instantly
questions.explanation: The book says BigQuery allows one write at a time and queues simultaneous writes.

questions.question: Why does the book call MongoDB a "variable-consistency" database?
options: Engineers have various configurable consistency options, both for the database and at the level of individual queries
It is always eventually consistent with no options
It is always strongly consistent with no options
Consistency cannot be configured in MongoDB
questions.explanation: The book describes MongoDB's configurable consistency options at database and query levels.

questions.question: How do object-storage-backed databases like BigQuery, Snowflake, and Databricks handle vacuuming differently?
options: In these databases the only downside of old data retention is storage cost: Snowflake users control a time-travel interval before auto-vacuuming, BigQuery uses a fixed seven-day history window, and Databricks retains data indefinitely until manually vacuumed to control S3 costs
They all vacuum automatically with no user control
They cannot vacuum at all
They retain data forever with no cost
questions.explanation: The book describes each database's retention/vacuuming behavior, including Snowflake time-travel and BigQuery's seven-day window.

questions.question: Why is vacuuming especially critical for relational databases like PostgreSQL and MySQL?
options: Large numbers of transactional operations can cause a rapid accumulation of dead records, so engineers must understand vacuuming's details and impact
They never accumulate dead records
Vacuuming is not supported in these databases
Transactions prevent dead records entirely
questions.explanation: The book says rapid dead-record accumulation makes vacuuming critical for PostgreSQL and MySQL.

questions.question: What does the book say about query results caching, and what example does it give?
options: Many cloud OLAP databases cache query results; a cold query that took 40 seconds might return in 1 second or less on rerun, reducing database pressure and improving user experience
Query caching never helps
Cached results are always stale and unusable
Databases never cache query results
questions.explanation: The book describes query results caching with the 40-second-to-1-second example.

questions.question: Why is querying an analytics database as a fast follower preferable to running analytics directly on the production database?
options: Production databases generally aren't equipped to handle production workloads and simultaneously run large analytics scans — such queries can slow the production application or even cause it to crash
Production databases are always faster for analytics
Analytics queries never affect production systems
Fast followers are always slower overall
questions.explanation: The book says production databases can be slowed or crashed by large analytics scans, so the fast-follower pattern minimizes production impact.

questions.question: What advantages does the book cite for using a proper OLAP-oriented system as a fast follower?
options: Both Druid and BigQuery combine a streaming buffer with long-term columnar storage in a Lambda-like setup, working extremely well for computing trailing statistics on vast historical data with near real-time updates
OLAP systems cannot act as followers
OLAP systems are always slower than transactional databases
Streaming buffers have no analytics value
questions.explanation: The book describes Druid/BigQuery's streaming-buffer-plus-columnar-storage fast-follower pattern.

questions.question: What is the principal idea of the Kappa architecture?
options: Handle all data like events and store them as a stream rather than a table, retaining events for extended periods (months or years) and querying them directly from streaming storage
Store all data in normalized tables
Treat streaming storage only as a short-term buffer
Reject all event-based data
questions.explanation: The book says Kappa's big idea is treating streaming storage as a real-time transport layer and a database for querying historical data.

questions.question: What tools does the book mention for querying data in the Kappa architecture?
options: Kafka KSQL supports aggregation, statistics, and sessionization; for more complex needs, external tools like Spark read a time range of data from Kafka; streaming storage can also feed Flink or Beam
Only SQL tables can be queried
Kappa architecture cannot be queried
Only batch tools work with Kappa
questions.explanation: The book describes Kafka KSQL and external tools like Spark, Flink, and Beam for Kappa querying.

questions.question: What fundamental limitation of traditional batch queries does the book describe, and how do streaming systems differ?
options: Batch queries generally treat the query engine as an external observer triggered by an actor (e.g. a cron job or dashboard), while most streaming systems support computations triggered directly from the data itself, emitting statistics when conditions are met
Batch queries can trigger themselves
Streaming systems never emit triggered statistics
Both paradigms are identical
questions.explanation: The book contrasts external-observer batch queries with data-triggered streaming computations.

questions.question: What is a session window, and how does it work in a streaming context?
options: It groups events that occur close together and filters out periods of inactivity; e.g. a session is any interval with no inactivity gap of five minutes or more, and session windows are per key
It is a fixed-length window with no gaps
It processes all data continuously without boundaries
Session windows are not per key
questions.explanation: The book describes session windows as inactivity-gap-based, per-key groupings, like a five-minute no-activity session timeout.

questions.question: What benefit does the book describe for making sessionization dynamic and near real-time?
options: With retrospective sessionization, actions could be automated a day or hour after a session closes; with dynamic sessionization, a user could get an immediately useful mobile alert based on their activity in the last 15 minutes
Dynamic sessionization is always slower
Retrospective sessionization is real-time
Sessionization has no business value
questions.explanation: The book contrasts retrospective and dynamic sessionization benefits.

questions.question: How does the book relate fixed-time (tumbling) windows to traditional batch ETL?
options: A tumbling window runs on a fixed schedule and processes all data since the previous window closed, similar to batch ETL jobs but generated more frequently with lower latency — batch is a special case of streaming
Tumbling windows have nothing to do with batch processing
Tumbling windows are always slower than daily ETL
Batch ETL cannot be described as windows
questions.explanation: The book says tumbling windows are similar to traditional batch ETL but more frequent and lower latency.

questions.question: How does the book describe a continuously sliding window with triggers?
options: The window may slide continuously but emit statistics only when certain conditions are met — e.g. a 30-second continuously sliding window that calculates a statistic only when a user clicks a particular banner, producing high output during clicks and none during lulls
Triggers are irrelevant to sliding windows
Continuously sliding windows always emit statistics
Sliding windows cannot use triggers
questions.explanation: The book describes trigger-based emission on a continuously sliding window using the banner-click example.

questions.question: What is the most basic approach to combining streams with other data, and how does enrichment differ?
options: The most basic approach is joining tables in a database where a stream feeds one or both tables; enrichment joins a stream to other data (e.g. a retailer enhancing partner events with product details and demographics via a serverless function looking up an in-memory database)
Enrichment never adds data to events
Streams can never be combined with tables
Joining tables is not possible
questions.explanation: The book describes table joins fed by streams and the enrichment pattern with a serverless function and in-memory cache.

questions.question: Where can the enrichment source for a stream originate, according to the book?
options: Almost anywhere — a table in a cloud data warehouse or RDBMS, or a file in object storage; it's a question of reading from the source and storing the enrichment data for retrieval by the stream
Only from a single hardcoded file
Only from the stream itself
Enrichment sources cannot exist
questions.explanation: The book says the enrichment source could originate almost anywhere.

questions.question: What complications does the book describe for stream-to-stream joining?
options: Streams may have significantly different latencies (e.g. an ad platform with a five-minute delay), and certain events may be delayed (e.g. a session-close event or an event from an offline phone), so typical architectures rely on streaming buffers with configurable retention
Stream-to-stream joins are trivial
All streams arrive with identical latency
Buffers are never needed for stream joins
questions.explanation: The book describes latency differences and streaming buffers for stream-to-stream joins.

questions.question: What is a data model, and what does a good one capture?
options: A data model represents the way data relates to the real world, reflecting how data must be structured and standardized to reflect the organization's processes, definitions, workflows, and logic — a good model captures how communication and work naturally flow
A data model is just a list of tables
Data models never reflect business logic
A good data model is haphazard and confusing
questions.explanation: The book defines a data model as representing how data relates to the real world and the organization's logic.

questions.question: How does the book illustrate that a good data model should correlate with business decisions?
options: A customer might mean different things to different departments — e.g. someone who bought in the last 30 days versus six months — and carefully defining this can massively impact customer-behavior reports or churn models where time since last purchase is critical
Business definitions are irrelevant to models
All departments define customers identically
Churn models never use purchase timing
questions.explanation: The book uses the customer-definition example to show modeling's business impact.

questions.question: What does the conceptual data model contain, and what tool is often used to visualize it?
options: Business logic and rules describing the system's data, such as schemas, tables, and fields; it's often visualized in an entity-relationship (ER) diagram encoding connections among entities like customers, orders, and products
Only physical storage configuration
Only SQL query syntax
Nothing — it is an empty placeholder
questions.explanation: The book describes the conceptual model's business logic and ER-diagram visualization.

questions.question: What does the logical data model add to the conceptual model?
options: Details how the conceptual model will be implemented, adding types for fields and mapping out primary and foreign keys
The final database configuration
Specific cloud regions
Nothing new
questions.explanation: The book says the logical model adds types and primary/foreign key mapping.

questions.question: What does the physical data model add?
options: How the logical model is implemented in a database system, adding specific databases, schemas, and tables including configuration details
Business rules and ER diagrams
Field types only
Nothing — it is identical to the conceptual model
questions.explanation: The book says the physical model adds concrete database implementation details.

questions.question: Who should be involved at the inception of data modeling, and what kind of activity does the book call it?
options: Business stakeholders should be involved to obtain definitions and business goals; modeling should be a full-contact sport whose goal is providing quality data for actionable insights and intelligent automation
Only data engineers should be involved
Stakeholders should be excluded
Modeling should happen without any business input
questions.explanation: The book says modeling is a full-contact sport involving business stakeholders from the start.

questions.question: What is grain in data modeling, and at what level is it typically set?
options: The resolution at which data is stored and queried, typically at the level of a primary key (customer ID, order ID, product ID), often accompanied by a date or timestamp for increased fidelity
The physical size of the database
The number of tables in the model
The network bandwidth of the warehouse
questions.explanation: The book defines grain as the resolution of stored/queried data at the primary-key level.

questions.question: What is normalization, and who first introduced it?
options: A database data modeling practice enforcing strict control over table/column relationships to remove data redundancy and ensure referential integrity — basically DRY applied to data — first introduced by Edgar Codd in the early 1970s
A technique for duplicating all data
A method for deleting tables
Introduced by Bill Inmon in 1989
questions.explanation: The book defines normalization as removing redundancy with referential integrity, introduced by Codd in the early 1970s.

questions.question: What are Codd's four main objectives of normalization?
options: Free relations from undesirable insertion/update/deletion dependencies, reduce the need for restructuring as new data types are introduced, make the relational model more informative to users, and make relations neutral to query statistics
Duplicate all data for safety
Reduce the number of tables
Eliminate primary keys
questions.explanation: The book lists Codd's four normalization objectives.

questions.question: What do the first three normal forms require?
options: 1NF: each column is unique with a single value and a unique primary key exists; 2NF: 1NF plus partial dependencies removed; 3NF: 2NF plus no transitive dependencies and only relevant fields related to the primary key
1NF requires denormalization
2NF adds transitive dependencies
3NF allows redundant data
questions.explanation: The book describes the sequential requirements of 1NF, 2NF, and 3NF.

questions.question: What is a partial dependency, and when can it occur?
options: A partial dependency occurs when a subset of fields in a composite key can determine a nonkey column; it can occur only when the primary key is composite
It occurs only with single-column keys
It is the same as a transitive dependency
It never occurs in normalized databases
questions.explanation: The book defines partial dependency as a subset of a composite key determining a nonkey column.

questions.question: What does the book say about denormalized data and the first normal form?
options: Denormalized data allows nested and redundant data; converting to 1NF removes repeats and nested data so fields contain single values
Denormalized data always satisfies 1NF
1NF allows nested objects
Denormalization is never mentioned
questions.explanation: The book describes denormalized as allowing nesting/redundancy and 1NF as removing them.

questions.question: By what convention does the book consider a database normalized?
options: A database is usually considered normalized if it's in third normal form, which is the convention used in the book
A database must reach 6NF
Any normal form counts as normalized
Databases are never considered normalized
questions.explanation: The book uses 3NF as the convention for normalized databases.

questions.question: What does the book say about denormalization as a performance strategy?
options: The degree of normalization depends on the use case, and although denormalization may seem like an antipattern, it's common in many OLAP systems storing semistructured data
Denormalization is always bad
All OLAP systems are fully normalized
Use case never affects normalization decisions
questions.explanation: The book says denormalization is common in OLAP semistructured systems despite seeming an antipattern.

questions.question: What was the goal of the data warehouse that Inmon created, and when?
options: Created in 1989, its goal was to separate the source system from the analytical system, since analysis on source systems bogged down production transactional databases with long-running queries
It was created to replace all source systems
It ran analytics directly on source systems
It was created in the 1970s
questions.explanation: The book says Inmon created the approach in 1989 to separate source and analytical systems.

questions.question: How does Inmon define a data warehouse, and what are its four critical parts?
options: A subject-oriented, integrated, nonvolatile, and time-variant collection of data in support of management's decisions
A collection of denormalized star schemas
A real-time operational store
A single table of all data
questions.explanation: The book quotes Inmon's definition with the four characteristics: subject-oriented, integrated, nonvolatile, and time-variant.

questions.question: What does the "integrated" characteristic of Inmon's data warehouse emphasize?
options: Data is fed from multiple disparate sources and converted, reformatted, resequenced, and summarized so the warehouse has a single physical corporate image — integration is the most important aspect
Each department keeps its own incompatible data
Data is never consolidated
Integration is the least important aspect
questions.explanation: The book says integration is the most important aspect, producing a single corporate image.

questions.question: How does Inmon's approach integrate and serve data, and what does it emphasize?
options: Data is integrated from across the organization into a granular, highly normalized (3NF) ER model with a relentless emphasis on ETL, then served to departments via business-specific data marts which may be denormalized
Data is served directly from source systems
It uses no data marts
It avoids ETL entirely
questions.explanation: The book describes Inmon's 3NF warehouse with ETL and downstream data marts.

questions.question: How does the book characterize Kimball's model relative to Inmon's in terms of integration and redundancy?
options: Kimball's bottom-up approach may enable faster iteration and modeling than Inmon, with the trade-off of potential looser data integration, data redundancy, and duplication
Kimball guarantees tighter integration than Inmon
Kimball eliminates all data redundancy
Kimball is always slower to iterate
questions.explanation: The book says Kimball enables faster iteration but with looser integration and more redundancy.

questions.question: What are the key properties of a fact table in a star schema?
options: Fact tables contain factual, quantitative, event-related data that is immutable and append-only, typically narrow and long, at the lowest grain possible, with each row representing the grain, and they reference only dimensions, not other fact tables
Fact tables are mutable and updated in place
Fact tables are wide and short
Fact tables reference other fact tables
questions.explanation: The book describes fact tables' quantitative, immutable, append-only, narrow-and-long, lowest-grain properties.

questions.question: Why are the data types in the book's example fact table all numeric?
options: Fact tables contain quantitative data and reference dimensions via keys, so strings describing events live in dimension tables rather than the fact table
Facts must never reference dimensions
Strings are forbidden in all databases
Fact tables can only store dates
questions.explanation: The book's example fact table uses integer/float keys and amounts, with attributes in dimensions.

questions.question: What do dimension tables provide, and what shape do they typically take?
options: Dimension tables provide reference data, attributes, and relational context for events, are smaller than fact tables, typically wide and short, and are denormalized with the possibility of duplicate data
They are narrow and long like facts
They must be strictly normalized
They contain only numeric values
questions.explanation: The book says dimensions are wide and short reference data, denormalized and possibly duplicated.

questions.question: What is a date dimension useful for, and what is its beauty?
options: It allows referencing a date key between fact and dimension tables to answer questions like total sales in a quarter or which weekday has more customers; its beauty is that you can add as many new fields as make sense
It can only store a single date per row
It cannot answer time-based questions
It is identical to a fact table
questions.explanation: The book describes the date dimension's analytic value and extensibility.

questions.question: What does an effective end date of 9999-01-01 in a Type 2 SCD indicate?
options: The customer record is active and hasn't changed
The customer was deleted
The record expired in the year 9999
The customer never existed
questions.explanation: The book says a 9999-01-01 end date means the record is active and unchanged.

questions.question: What are the three most common types of slowly changing dimensions?
options: Type 1 overwrites existing records losing history; Type 2 keeps a full history by inserting new records; Type 3 is similar to Type 2 but creates a new field rather than a new row
Type 1 keeps full history; Type 2 overwrites; Type 3 deletes records
All three types are identical
Type 3 creates a new table each change
questions.explanation: The book describes SCD Types 1, 2, and 3, with Type 1 the default and Type 2 most common in practice.

questions.question: What is a star schema, and what advantages does it offer?
options: A fact table surrounded by the necessary dimensions representing the data model of the business; it results in fewer joins than highly normalized models (speeding up queries) and is arguably easier for business users to understand and use
A single normalized table
A model requiring many joins
A schema that is hard for business users to use
questions.explanation: The book describes the star schema's fewer joins and business-user-friendliness.

questions.question: What is a conformed dimension, and why does the book recommend reducing the number of dimensions?
options: A dimension reused across multiple star schemas sharing the same fields, allowing multiple fact tables to be combined; reducing dimensions helps reuse reference data and avoid replicating dimensions, which can drift business definitions
A dimension unique to one star schema
A dimension that cannot be shared
Replicating dimensions is always best
questions.explanation: The book defines conformed dimensions and warns against replicating dimensions to avoid definition drift.

questions.question: What does the book say about applying the Kimball data model to streaming data?
options: The Kimball model is appropriate only for batch data and not for streaming data
Kimball works perfectly for streaming
Kimball is the recommended streaming model
All models work for streaming equally
questions.explanation: The book says Kimball is appropriate only for batch, not streaming.

questions.question: What is the Data Vault methodology, and how does it load data?
options: Created in the 1990s by Dan Linstedt, it separates the structural aspects of source data from its attributes and simply loads data from source systems directly into purpose-built tables in an insert-only manner, with no notion of good, bad, or conformed data
It models business logic in facts and dimensions
It overwrites data in place
It was created by Ralph Kimball
questions.explanation: The book describes the Data Vault's insert-only loading and lack of conformed data notions.

questions.question: What standard fields does a hub in a Data Vault always contain?
options: Hash key, load date, record source, and business key(s)
Only a business key
Descriptive attributes only
A foreign key to a satellite
questions.explanation: The book lists the hub's standard fields: hash key, load date, record source, and business keys.

questions.question: Why is a hub insert-only, and how do queries typically proceed?
options: Once data is loaded into a hub it's permanent and not altered; a user will query a hub, which links to a satellite table containing the query's relevant attributes
Hubs are constantly updated in place
Queries never touch hubs
Hubs contain descriptive context
questions.explanation: The book says hubs are insert-only and queries flow from hub to satellite for attributes.

questions.question: What do link tables do in a Data Vault, and what shape are they?
options: They track the relationships of business keys between hubs, ideally at the lowest possible grain, and are many-to-many; creating a new link represents a new relationship
They store descriptive attributes
They are one-to-one only
They cannot change over time
questions.explanation: The book describes links as many-to-many relationship tables between hubs.

questions.question: What are the only required fields in a satellite?
options: A primary key consisting of the business key of the parent hub and a load date
Descriptive attributes only
A hash key and record source
Nothing is required
questions.explanation: The book says satellites require only the parent hub business key and a load date.

questions.question: What other Data Vault table types does the book mention but not cover in depth?
options: Point-in-time (PIT) and bridge tables
Fact and dimension tables
Star and snowflake tables
Broadcast and shuffle tables
questions.explanation: The book mentions PIT and bridge tables as other comprehensive Data Vault components.

questions.question: When is business logic applied in a Data Vault, and how can the model be used with other techniques?
options: Business logic is created and interpreted when data is queried; the Data Vault is often a landing zone for analytical data that is later modeled in a warehouse, commonly using a star schema, and can also be adapted for NoSQL and streaming
Business logic is enforced at load time
The Data Vault cannot combine with other techniques
It only works with Kimball models
questions.explanation: The book says Data Vault business logic is applied at query time and it can precede star schemas or adapt to NoSQL/streaming.

questions.question: Why are relaxed modeling approaches like wide tables becoming more common?
options: Cloud storage is dirt cheap — cheaper to store data than agonize over the optimum representation — and the popularity of nested data like JSON means schemas are flexible
Cloud storage is expensive
Nested data forces rigid schemas
Modeling rigor is now free
questions.explanation: The book cites cheap storage and flexible nested schemas as reasons for relaxed modeling.

questions.question: How do wide tables typically arise, and how does schema evolution differ between relational and columnar databases?
options: Wide tables generally arise through schema evolution as engineers gradually add fields; adding a field in a relational database is slow and resource-heavy, while in a columnar database it's initially just a metadata change with new files added to the column
Wide tables are always designed up front
Schema evolution is fast in relational databases
Columnar databases cannot add fields
questions.explanation: The book contrasts schema evolution's cost in relational versus columnar databases.

questions.question: Why do analytics queries on wide tables often run faster than equivalent queries on normalized data?
options: Removing joins can have a huge impact on scan performance since the wide table contains all the data that would have been joined in a more rigorous approach, with facts and dimensions in the same table
Wide tables require more joins
Normalized data is always faster to scan
Joins never affect scan performance
questions.explanation: The book says wide tables speed analytics by eliminating joins.

questions.question: What criticisms does the book list for wide denormalized tables?
options: The biggest criticism is that as you blend data you lose business logic in analytics, and another downside is the performance of updates to elements like an array field can be very painful
Wide tables preserve all business logic
Array updates are always fast
There are no criticisms
questions.explanation: The book lists losing business logic and painful array-element updates as criticisms.

questions.question: When does the book suggest using a wide table?
options: When you don't care about data modeling, or when you have a lot of data needing more flexibility than traditional rigor provides; wide tables also lend themselves to streaming data
Only for strictly governed datasets
Never — wide tables are always wrong
Only for tiny datasets
questions.explanation: The book suggests wide tables when modeling rigor isn't needed or flexibility is required.

questions.question: What questions should you consider if you choose not to model your data and query source systems directly?
options: How do I know query results are consistent? Do I have proper definitions of business logic in the source system? What query load am I putting on my source systems and how does this impact their users?
How much does modeling cost?
Which modeling tool is best?
None — direct querying is always ideal
questions.explanation: The book lists consistency, business definitions, and source-system query load as considerations.

questions.question: Why is translating batch modeling techniques like Kimball to streaming tricky or impossible?
options: Because of the unbounded and continuous nature of streaming data — e.g. how would you continuously update a Type-2 SCD without bringing your warehouse to its knees?
Streaming data is bounded and discrete
Kimball works perfectly for streaming
SCDs never need updating in streaming
questions.explanation: The book says streaming's unbounded nature makes batch techniques like Kimball tricky, using the Type-2 SCD example.

questions.question: What do streaming data experts overwhelmingly suggest for modeling streaming data?
options: Anticipate changes in source data and keep a flexible schema — assume source systems provide correct data with the right business definitions as they exist today, store recent and historical data so they can be queried together, and create automation that responds to anomalies
Use a rigid fixed schema
Ignore schema changes entirely
Never store historical streaming data
questions.explanation: The book summarizes expert advice: flexible schema, assume correct sources, combined storage, and anomaly automation.

questions.question: How does a transformation differ from a query?
options: A query retrieves data based on filtering and join logic; a transformation persists results for consumption by additional transformations or queries, and transformations also differ in complexity, combining data from multiple sources and reusing intermediate results
Transformations never persist results
Queries persist all their results
They are identical operations
questions.explanation: The book contrasts queries (retrieve) with transformations (persist + complex pipelines).

questions.question: What undercurrent do transformations critically rely on?
options: Orchestration — it combines many discrete operations such as intermediate transformations that store data temporarily or permanently for downstream consumption
Security
Only networking
No undercurrent is involved
questions.explanation: The book says transformations critically rely on orchestration.

questions.question: What is the basic idea behind distributed joins, and when is a broadcast join possible?
options: Break a logical join into much smaller node joins on individual servers; in the best case one side of the join is small enough to fit on a single node, enabling a broadcast join, otherwise a more resource-intensive shuffle hash join is required
Distributed joins always run on one node
Broadcast joins require both tables to be large
Shuffle hash joins are always cheapest
questions.explanation: The book describes splitting joins into node joins, with broadcast when a side fits on one node.

questions.question: What are top priorities in query optimizers for join performance, and what can prefiltering achieve?
options: Join reordering — applying filters early and moving small tables to the left for left joins can dramatically reduce processed data; prefiltering data to create broadcast joins where possible can dramatically improve performance and reduce resource consumption
Filters should be applied as late as possible
Join reordering is unimportant
Prefiltering always hurts performance
questions.explanation: The book recommends early filters and join reordering to reduce processed data.

questions.question: How does a shuffle hash join work?
options: When neither table fits on a single node, a hashing scheme repartitions both tables by join key across the cluster, reshuffles data to the appropriate nodes, and joins the new partitions
It sends one table to all nodes
It joins data on a single node
It avoids all data movement
questions.explanation: The book describes the hashing/repartition/reshuffle mechanics of shuffle hash joins.

questions.question: Why was the traditional ETL pattern developed, and what drove it?
options: It was driven by the limitations of both source and target systems: the extract phase tended to be a major bottleneck with source RDBMS constraints, and transformation ran in a dedicated system because the target was extremely resource-constrained in storage and CPU
It was driven by unlimited resources
Target systems were powerful enough to transform
ETL required no extraction
questions.explanation: The book attributes ETL to source extraction bottlenecks and resource-constrained targets.

questions.question: What is ELT, and how did the data-lake version of it differ from the warehouse version?
options: As warehouses grew in performance, ELT extracts raw data, imports it with minimal transformation, and transforms in the warehouse; the data-lake version loads massive quantities with no preparation or plan, assuming transformation happens later — a great recipe for a data swamp
ELT always transforms before loading
The data-lake version transforms immediately
ELT is never used in data lakes
questions.explanation: The book describes both ELT versions and the swamp risk of unplanned lake loading, citing Inmon.

questions.question: How does the book say ETL and ELT should be applied today?
options: The terms should be applied only at the micro level within individual transformation pipelines rather than at the macro level for a whole organization, since organizations can apply the proper technique case by case
Every organization must choose one macro pattern
ETL and ELT are never applied at the micro level
The terms are meaningless
questions.explanation: The book recommends applying ETL/ELT at the micro level per pipeline.

questions.question: What does the book say about SQL being declarative and its ability to build complex workflows?
options: SQL is declarative — writers stipulate final data characteristics and the compiler/optimizer determine steps — but it can effectively build complex DAGs using common table expressions, SQL scripts, or an orchestration tool
Declarative languages cannot build complex pipelines
SQL is a procedural language
SQL cannot use CTEs or orchestration
questions.explanation: The book says SQL is declarative but can build complex DAGs with CTEs, scripts, or orchestration.

questions.question: What three questions does the book suggest asking to decide between native Spark and Spark SQL?
options: How difficult is it to code the transformation in SQL? How readable and maintainable will the resulting SQL code be? Should some of the transformation code be pushed into a custom library for future reuse?
How many nodes should the cluster use?
Which cloud provider is cheapest?
SQL questions are irrelevant
questions.explanation: The book lists these three questions for choosing between Spark SQL and native Spark.

questions.question: What example does the book give of a transformation better suited to a procedural language than SQL?
options: Word stemming — it could be implemented in SQL by joining against a suffix table and using parsing/substring functions, but this is extremely complex with numerous edge cases and neither readable nor maintainable
Simple column selection
Counting rows in a table
Filtering by a date range
questions.explanation: The book uses word stemming as an example where native Spark is better than awkward SQL.

questions.question: What does the book say about SQL's notion of libraries and reusable code?
options: SQL doesn't include a natural notion of libraries or reusable code, though some engines allow UDFs as objects inside a database; reusable libraries are easy to create in Spark and PySpark, and SQL can be recycled by committing results to tables/views or via dbt templating
SQL has excellent library support
UDFs can be committed to Git automatically
Spark has no reusable libraries
questions.explanation: The book describes SQL's library limitations and the recycling options of tables/views, orchestration, and dbt.

questions.question: What top-level recommendations does the book give for coding in native Spark?
options: Filter early and often, rely heavily on the core Spark API and understand the native way of doing things, be careful with UDFs, and consider intermixing SQL
Filter late, avoid the core API
Use UDFs for everything
Never use SQL with Spark
questions.explanation: The book lists these four recommendations for native Spark coding.

questions.question: Why should PySpark users be especially careful with Python UDFs?
options: PySpark is an API wrapper for Scala Spark, and running Python UDFs forces data to be passed to Python where processing is less efficient; if you must use UDFs, consider rewriting them in Scala or Java to improve performance
Python UDFs are always the fastest option
PySpark doesn't use a JVM at all
Python UDFs never pass data to Python
questions.explanation: The book explains PySpark's Scala-wrapper architecture and the cost of Python UDFs.

questions.question: What is one benefit of using SQL with Spark?
options: SQL allows taking advantage of the Spark Catalyst optimizer, which may squeeze out more performance than native Spark code, and SQL is often easier to write and maintain for simple operations
SQL disables the optimizer
Native Spark is always faster than SQL
SQL cannot be combined with native Spark
questions.explanation: The book says SQL leverages the Catalyst optimizer and is simpler for basic operations.

questions.question: What is the truncate-and-reload update pattern?
options: Truncate wipes the old data without updating anything, and transformations are rerun and loaded into the cleared table, effectively generating a new table version
It updates individual records in place
It inserts new records without clearing
It deletes only expired records
questions.explanation: The book describes truncate-and-reload as clearing a table and rerunning transformations.

questions.question: What are the downsides of an insert-only update pattern, and what alternative does the book suggest?
options: Finding the latest record at query time can be extremely computationally expensive; alternatively, use a materialized view, an insert-only table maintaining all records, and a truncate-and-reload target table holding the current state for serving
Insert-only is always cheap at query time
Materialized views cannot help
There are no alternatives
questions.explanation: The book describes the expensive latest-record lookup and the materialized-view/truncate-reload alternative.

questions.question: What does the book say about single-row inserts into columnar OLAP databases?
options: It is an antipattern that puts a massive load on the system, causes data to be written in many separate files inefficient for reads, and requires reclustering later; load data in a periodic micro-batch or batch fashion instead
Single-row inserts are ideal for columnar databases
Single-row inserts write efficient files
Batching is never recommended
questions.explanation: The book calls single-row inserts an antipattern and recommends micro-batch/batch loading.

questions.question: What exception does the book mention to the advice not to insert frequently?
options: The enhanced Lambda architecture used by BigQuery and Apache Druid, which hybridizes a streaming buffer with columnar storage
No exceptions exist
All databases should avoid streaming buffers
The exception is single-row inserts in row databases
questions.explanation: The book cites BigQuery/Druid's streaming-buffer-plus-columnar hybrid as the exception.

questions.question: Why are deletes more expensive in columnar systems and data lakes?
options: In columnar systems and data lakes, deletes are more expensive than inserts
Deletes are free in all systems
Columnar systems delete instantly
Deletes are cheaper than inserts everywhere
questions.explanation: The book states deletes are more expensive than inserts in columnar systems and data lakes.

questions.question: Why does the book say upsert/merge patterns cause the most trouble for teams transitioning from row-based to columnar cloud systems?
options: Upsert/merge was designed for row-based databases where updates look up and change records in place, while file-based systems use copy on write (COW), so if one record in a file changes, the whole file must be rewritten with the new changes
Row-based databases also use copy on write
File-based systems support in-place updates
COW never rewrites files
questions.explanation: The book explains the mismatch between row-based in-place updates and file-based copy-on-write.

questions.question: How does copy-on-write (COW) actually operate in modern columnar systems, and when are merges performant?
options: COW seldom entails rewriting the whole table — it can operate at various resolutions (partition, cluster, block) — and merges can be extremely performant for large update sets, even outperforming transactional databases
COW always rewrites the entire table
Merges are never performant
COW resolution is always whole-table
questions.explanation: The book describes COW at partition/cluster/block resolution and large-merge performance.

questions.question: What approaches does the book mention to bring columnar databases closer to real time?
options: BigQuery allows streaming inserts into a table with specialized materialized views presenting an efficient near real-time deduplicated view; Druid uses two-tier storage and SSDs to support ultrafast real-time queries
Columnar databases cannot approach real time
Druid has no real-time capability
BigQuery disallows streaming inserts
questions.explanation: The book describes BigQuery streaming-plus-materialized-view and Druid's two-tier SSD approach.

questions.question: Why does the book say updating the schema is easier in columnar systems than row-based ones?
options: Columns can typically be added, deleted, and renamed easily, and adding a field in a columnar database is initially just a metadata change
Columnar schemas are fixed forever
Row-based databases update schemas instantly
Schema changes are equally hard everywhere
questions.explanation: The book says columnar systems make schema updates easier.

questions.question: What organizational challenges does the book raise about schema management, and what is a table fork?
options: Will schema updates be automated (like Fivetran) risking downstream breaks? Is there a straightforward review process? Will SELECT * queries break? How long will changes take? A table fork is a new table version specific to a project
Schema management is always automatic
SELECT * is good practice in columnar databases
Table forks are not mentioned
questions.explanation: The book raises these schema-management questions and defines the table fork.

questions.question: What new option does the book describe for semistructured JSON data in cloud data warehouses?
options: Store raw JSON in a field while storing frequently accessed data in adjacent flattened fields, taking extra storage but allowing flattened convenience with semistructured flexibility; frequently accessed JSON data can be added into the schema over time
Store only flattened columns and discard JSON
JSON cannot be stored in warehouses
Flattened fields are forbidden
questions.explanation: The book describes the raw-JSON-plus-flattened-fields hybrid approach.

questions.question: What is data wrangling, and how does the book describe the typical process?
options: Data wrangling takes messy, malformed data and turns it into useful, clean data, generally as a batch transformation — e.g. ingesting EDI data, often as a single text-field table, then writing queries to parse and break it apart, discovering anomalies over time
Data wrangling only compresses data
Data wrangling is always real-time
Wrangled data needs no parsing
questions.explanation: The book describes the messy-to-clean wrangling process with the EDI example.

questions.question: How does the book suggest thinking about data-wrangling tools, and what features do they typically have?
options: Think of them as integrated development environments (IDEs) for malformed data; they present a sample of data in a visual interface with inferred types, statistics, distributions, anomalies, and nulls, letting users add processing steps and push jobs to scalable systems like Spark
They are always no-code toys with no value
They cannot push jobs to Spark
They never show data statistics
questions.explanation: The book reframes wrangling tools as IDEs for malformed data with visual/statistical features.

questions.question: What business logic example does the book give for derived data, and what criticism does it address?
options: The example is nuanced profit calculations (before/after marketing costs) integrating an attribution model; critics say maintaining consistency in derived metrics is hard since attribution changes must be merged into many ETL scripts, but the alternative — analysts running reporting queries with profit logic — is even more impractical
Derived data needs no maintenance
Attribution models never change
ETL scripts never break the DRY principle
questions.explanation: The book describes the profit/attribution derived-data example and the criticism trade-off.

questions.question: What alternative does the book mention for pushing business logic into a dedicated layer?
options: Push business logic into a metrics layer that encodes business logic and lets analysts build analytics from a library of defined metrics, while still leveraging the data warehouse for computational heavy lifting
Remove all business logic from analytics
Metrics layers replace data warehouses entirely
Analysts should write raw queries with logic each time
questions.explanation: The book describes the metrics layer approach for business logic.

questions.question: What is MapReduce, and what does a simple job consist of?
options: A batch transformation pattern introduced by Google consisting of map tasks that read data blocks, a shuffle that redistributes results by key across the cluster, and a reduce step that aggregates data on each node
A single-node processing framework
A streaming-only pattern
A database index structure
questions.explanation: The book describes MapReduce's map/shuffle/reduce stages, introduced by Google.

questions.question: Why is the map portion of a MapReduce job described as embarrassingly parallel?
options: Each map task runs a query on a single data block independently, so the data scan rate across the cluster scales essentially linearly with the number of nodes
Map tasks must coordinate globally
Map tasks run sequentially
The scan rate never scales
questions.explanation: The book says map tasks on individual blocks scale linearly with nodes.

questions.question: Why is Google's original MapReduce model viewed as excessively rigid?
options: It utilizes numerous short-lived ephemeral tasks that read from and write to disk, with no intermediate state preserved in memory — all data is transferred between tasks by disk or network, driving high disk bandwidth and increasing processing time
It preserves all state in memory
It avoids disk entirely
It is the fastest possible model
questions.explanation: The book describes MapReduce's disk-heavy ephemeral-task model as rigid.

questions.question: How does post-MapReduce processing differ from the original model?
options: It retains map, shuffle, and reduce elements but relaxes constraints to allow in-memory caching, dramatically speeding up specific tasks; Spark and BigQuery treat data as a distributed set residing in memory, spilling to disk as a second-class layer when memory overflows
It discards map and reduce entirely
It forbids in-memory caching
It treats disk as the primary processing layer
questions.explanation: The book describes post-MapReduce in-memory caching and disk-as-second-class processing.

questions.question: What three roles do (nonmaterialized) views play in a database, per the book?
options: Security (selecting specific columns/filtering rows for restricted access), providing a current deduplicated picture of data for insert-only patterns, and presenting common data access patterns like prejoined wide tables
Storing raw data
Enforcing primary keys
Only dashboard rendering
questions.explanation: The book describes views' security, deduplication, and common-pattern roles.

questions.question: How can materialized views serve a query optimization role even for queries that don't reference them?
options: Many query optimizers can identify queries that look like a materialized view and rewrite the query to select from the precomputed results
Materialized views are never used by optimizers
Optimizers cannot rewrite queries
Materialized views only serve when directly referenced
questions.explanation: The book describes optimizers rewriting similar queries to use materialized view results.

questions.question: What is composable materialized views, and what Databricks feature supports it?
options: In general materialized views don't allow composition (a materialized view can't select from another), but Databricks introduced live tables where each table is updated as data arrives and data flows down to subsequent tables asynchronously
All materialized views support composition
Live tables never update
Databricks does not support live tables
questions.explanation: The book describes Databricks live tables as composable materialized views.

questions.question: What are federated queries, and what example does the book give?
options: A database feature allowing an OLAP database to select from external data sources such as object storage or RDBMS; e.g. a data warehouse issues a federated query to object storage, MySQL, and PostgreSQL and returns combined results
Queries that only read local tables
A security protocol for queries
A type of index
questions.explanation: The book describes federated queries across object storage and RDBMS sources.

questions.question: What are Snowflake external tables, and how do they work?
