options: External tables are defined on S3 buckets with an external data location and file format; data is not ingested into the table, but when queried Snowflake reads from S3 and processes based on the creation parameters, and the S3 data can even be joined to internal tables
External tables copy all data into Snowflake
External tables cannot be joined
External tables store data only in memory
questions.explanation: The book describes Snowflake's external tables reading from S3 without ingestion.

questions.question: What is data virtualization, and which systems exemplify it?
options: A data processing and query system that doesn't store data internally — Trino (e.g. Starburst) and Presto are examples par excellence; the most significant considerations are supported external sources and performance
A system that stores all data internally
A system with no external sources
A physical storage array
questions.explanation: The book defines data virtualization with Trino/Presto examples.

questions.question: What is query pushdown, and what two purposes does it serve?
options: Moving as much work as possible to source databases, e.g. pushing filtering predicates into source queries; it offloads computation from the virtualization layer and reduces the quantity of data that must cross the network
Moving all work to the virtualization layer
Increasing network data transfer
Disabling source query performance
questions.explanation: The book describes query pushdown's computation offload and network reduction benefits.

questions.question: Why should data virtualization not be used haphazardly, and how can it be used as an ingestion component?
options: Virtualizing a production MySQL database doesn't solve the problem of analytics queries impacting production since Trino pulls from MySQL every time; it can instead be used to select from MySQL once a day at midnight, saving results to S3 for downstream transformations and protecting MySQL
Data virtualization always solves production load issues
Trino caches data between queries
Data virtualization cannot be used in pipelines
questions.explanation: The book warns about virtualization's production impact and describes the ingestion-component usage.

questions.question: How does data virtualization relate to the data mesh concept?
options: Virtualization expands the data lake to many more sources by abstracting away barriers that silo data, and can serve as a critical access layer for practical sharing in a data mesh where small teams prepare and share data
Virtualization prevents data sharing
Data mesh never uses virtualization
Virtualization and data mesh are unrelated
questions.explanation: The book connects virtualization to data mesh sharing.

questions.question: What is the difference between streaming queries and streaming transformations?
options: Streaming queries run dynamically to present a current view of data, while streaming transformations aim to prepare data for downstream consumption — e.g. enriching IoT events with device metadata from a separate database
They are identical concepts
Streaming transformations present current views
Streaming queries prepare downstream data
questions.explanation: The book contrasts streaming queries (current view) with streaming transformations (prepare downstream).

questions.question: What is a streaming DAG, and how do Pulsar and Kafka/Flink differ in supporting it?
options: A streaming DAG enriches, merges, and splits multiple streams in real time (e.g. combining clickstream and IoT data); building one with Kafka and Flink long meant a complex Rube Goldberg machine of topics and jobs, while Pulsar treats DAGs as a core streaming abstraction defined as code inside a single system
Streaming DAGs are only for batch
Kafka treats DAGs as a core abstraction
Pulsar cannot define DAGs
questions.explanation: The book describes streaming DAGs and contrasts Kafka+Flink complexity with Pulsar's native DAG support.

questions.question: What are the characteristics of micro-batching, and how often might it run?
options: Micro-batching takes a batch-oriented framework and applies it in a streaming situation, running anywhere from every two minutes to every second; frameworks like Spark Streaming are designed for this and perform well with appropriate resources at high frequency
Micro-batching runs once a day maximum
Micro-batching processes one event at a time
Micro-batching cannot use batch frameworks
questions.explanation: The book describes micro-batching's frequency range and Spark Streaming suitability.

questions.question: How does the book describe true streaming systems and their trade-offs?
options: True streaming systems like Beam and Flink are designed to process one event at a time, but this comes with significant overhead, and even in true streaming systems many processes still occur in batches such as windows and triggers
True streaming processes only batches
True streaming has no overhead
Beam and Flink never use windows
questions.explanation: The book describes event-at-a-time processing with overhead and residual batching.

questions.question: What examples does the book give for choosing micro-batching versus true streaming?
options: For Black Friday sales metrics published every few minutes, micro-batches are probably fine; if an ops team is computing metrics every second to detect DDoS attacks, true streaming may be in order
DDoS detection should always use micro-batches
Black Friday metrics need true streaming
Use case never matters
questions.explanation: The book contrasts the Black Friday (micro-batch) and DDoS (true streaming) scenarios.

questions.question: What does the book say about vendor benchmarks in the micro-batch versus streaming debate?
options: Watch out for spurious vendor benchmarks — vendors are notorious for cherry-picking benchmarks and artificial examples that don't match reality, showing massive advantages that fail to deliver in the real world for your use case
Vendor benchmarks are always reliable
All benchmarks are identical
Vendors never run benchmarks
questions.explanation: The book warns against cherry-picked vendor benchmarks.

questions.question: Who does the book identify as upstream stakeholders for transformations, and how do they split?
options: Upstream stakeholders split into those who control the business definitions and those who control the systems generating data; engineers must know data sources, their use, and the business logic involved
Only data engineers
Only business stakeholders
Only downstream consumers
questions.explanation: The book splits upstream stakeholders into business-definition and data-system controllers.

questions.question: What do upstream stakeholders want regarding your queries and transformations?
options: They want to make sure your queries and transformations minimally impact their systems, and they expect bidirectional communication about data model changes like column and index changes that can affect queries and transformations
They want maximum query load on their systems
They never communicate schema changes
They want no communication at all
questions.explanation: The book says upstream stakeholders want minimal impact and bidirectional schema-change communication.

questions.question: Who are the downstream stakeholders, and what do they expect from transformed data?
options: Data analysts, data scientists, ML engineers, and the business; queries should execute as quickly as possible cost-effectively, and users should be confident data is high quality and complete so it can be integrated into workflows and data products
Only executives
Only the data engineering team
Nobody — data is self-serve
questions.explanation: The book describes downstream stakeholders' performance and quality expectations.

questions.question: What security considerations does the book raise for the transformation stage?
options: Control who has access to new combined datasets including column, row, and cell-level access; monitor read/write privileges and query-time attack vectors; keep credentials hidden from code; and never allow unsecured data to traverse the public internet
Security is only relevant at ingestion
Credentials can be pasted into code
Public internet data needs no encryption
questions.explanation: The book describes dataset access control, credential hygiene, and encrypted transit.

questions.question: Why is data management especially critical at the transformation stage?
options: Transformation inherently creates new datasets that need to be managed; naming conventions must align with business definitions, data catalogs provide clarity on fields, and definitional accuracy ensures transformations adhere to expected business logic
Transformations create no new data
Naming conventions are unimportant
Data catalogs are not used for clarity
questions.explanation: The book emphasizes new-dataset management, naming conventions, catalogs, and definitional accuracy.

questions.question: How do MDM and data lineage tools support transformations?
options: MDM preserves data's original integrity and ground truth for conformed dimensions and transformations; data lineage tools help engineers understand previous transformation steps and help analysts understand where data came from
MDM and lineage are unrelated to transformations
Lineage only helps analysts, never engineers
MDM corrupts data integrity
questions.explanation: The book describes MDM's ground-truth role and lineage tools' benefits.

questions.question: What regulatory questions does the book raise about data models and transformations?
options: Are sensitive fields masked or obfuscated? Can you delete data in response to deletion requests? Does lineage tracking let you see data derived from deleted data and rerun transformations to remove it downstream?
Regulations never affect transformations
Deletion requests can be ignored
Lineage is not needed for deletions
questions.explanation: The book raises masking, deletion, and downstream-lineage compliance questions.

questions.question: What are the two areas of concern for DataOps with queries and transformations?
options: Data and systems — monitor and alert on changes or anomalies in both, with the field of data observability exploding and even a job title of data reliability engineer
Only data quality
Only system uptime
Only security
questions.explanation: The book says DataOps has data and systems areas of concern.

questions.question: What data-side checks does the book recommend for DataOps at the query/transformation stage?
options: Run data-quality tests on input and transformed datasets checking schema, shape, min/max values, and null counts; if there's a quality issue, flag it, roll back the changes, and investigate root cause
Only check query syntax
Data-quality tests are unnecessary
Rollbacks are never possible
questions.explanation: The book describes input/output data-quality tests and rollback capability.

questions.question: What ops-side metrics does the book say to monitor for query and transformation systems?
options: Query queue length, query concurrency, memory usage, storage utilization, network latency, and disk I/O — use metric data to spot bottlenecks and poor-performing queries for refactoring and tuning
Only CPU temperature
Only the number of tables
System metrics are irrelevant
questions.explanation: The book lists these ops metrics for spotting bottlenecks.

questions.question: How does the shift toward SaaS-based analytical databases change the cost profile of data consumption?
options: On-premises warehouses were purchased up front with no usage cost, while cloud warehouses charge on a consumption basis, so engineers must focus on cost management and cost optimization — the practice of FinOps
Cloud warehouses are always cheaper with no monitoring
Cost management is unnecessary in the cloud
Consumption pricing has no cost implications
questions.explanation: The book contrasts up-front on-premises costs with consumption-based cloud costs and FinOps.

questions.question: What architecture example does the book give of using the wrong pipelines and databases?
options: A data team might connect a real-time data pipeline to an RDBMS or Elasticsearch and use it as their data warehouse — these systems are not optimized for high-volume aggregated OLAP queries and will implode under the workload
RDBMS systems are ideal OLAP warehouses
Elasticsearch handles OLAP aggregates well
Architecture choices never affect query performance
questions.explanation: The book warns about using transactional/search systems as OLAP warehouses.

questions.question: What does the book say about managing transformation pipelines with time-based schedules versus orchestration?
options: Simple time-based schedules like cron work reasonably well at first but turn into a nightmare as workflows grow; use orchestration to manage complex pipelines with a dependency-based approach, since orchestration is the glue spanning multiple systems
Cron jobs scale perfectly forever
Orchestration only works for single systems
Dependency-based scheduling is worse than cron
questions.explanation: The book recommends dependency-based orchestration over time-based schedules.

questions.question: What does the book say about UDFs versus native functions in transformation code?
options: Know the best practices of your tools — e.g. are you using a UDF when a native function might work much better? Poorly written, sluggish UDFs can be replaced by a built-in SQL command with instant dramatic improvement
UDFs are always the best choice
Native functions never outperform UDFs
UDFs need no optimization
questions.explanation: The book recommends native functions over poorly written UDFs.

questions.question: What is analytics engineering, and what role does the data engineer play in it?
options: Analytics engineering brings software engineering practices to end users with analytics as code; tools like dbt let analysts write in-database transformations in SQL without a DBA, and the data engineer is responsible for setting up the code repository and CI/CD pipeline used by analysts and scientists
Analytics engineering replaces data engineers entirely
dbt requires no SQL
Data engineers never set up CI/CD
questions.explanation: The book describes analytics engineering and the data engineer's CI/CD role.

questions.question: What does the book caution about GUI-based low-code transformation tools?
options: They generate SQL or another language behind the scenes, and while the point is to avoid low-level details, understanding the generated code helps with debugging and performance optimization — blindly assuming the tool generates performant code is a mistake
Generated code is always performant
Low-code tools need no understanding
The generated code can never be inspected
questions.explanation: The book warns against blindly trusting low-code tool-generated code.

questions.question: What final advice does the book give about the purpose of transformations?
options: Engineers are not hired to play with the latest technological toys but to serve their customers — transformations are where data adds value and ROI to the business
Technological toys are the priority
Customer value is secondary
Transformations never add business value
questions.explanation: The book emphasizes serving customers and business ROI as transformations' purpose.

questions.question: What does the book say about identifying streaming use cases before choosing technologies?
options: Engineering teams that think about real-time data as technology for its own sake will repeat the mistakes of the big data era; the majority of organizations have a business use case that would benefit from streaming, so identify the value before choosing technologies and complex systems
Choose technology first, find use cases later
Streaming has no business use cases
Value identification is unnecessary
questions.explanation: The book advises identifying streaming value before technology choices.
